title: What Haru Saw
part: PART FOUR: THE NIGHT OF THE NORTH WIND

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 19. Today's news: the whole truth is heavier than half of it.*

The shop was so quiet that Haru could hear the snow settling on the roof tiles. The drying lines hung still, pale sheets motionless in the cold air. She stood in the center of the room, her fingers drumming against the edge of the printing bench. Her father, her mother, and her grandfather waited.

"The spark came out of the furnace door, and the wind carried it," Haru said. Her voice stayed steady, though her hands trembled inside her sleeves. "I saw the crack in the cap. I saw the pile of cherry-wood shavings right next to the furnace. And I saw the ash door. It was open."

She swallowed, the taste of dry paper dust in her mouth. The air felt heavy, thick with unspoken things.

"And I saw Shin," she continued, looking at her father. "He was holding a bucket. He was so tired. He was only nine." She looked down at her feet. "If I print this, everyone will know it was Shin. He left the door open. If I do not print it, then my sheet is only half a truth."

Kichi, who had been sitting on the bench, stopped chewing his cold rice cake. He looked at Haru with wide eyes, the crumb forgotten on his chin.

"The half truth," Haru whispered, "is still a lie."
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron with a vermilion cord in her topknot, stands in the center of a dim print shop with her hands clasped, while Kichi, a gangly boy in a moss-green coat, looks on with a paused rice cake in his hand, blank paper hanging on lines above them.

pages.text:
Grandfather Tobei rubbed his bad shoulder. His eyes stayed fixed on the knife resting on the table.

"A half truth," he said, his voice dry as old wood, "is a lie that has learned to be quiet. It is not better. It is just smaller."

Mother Okiyo stepped forward. She placed a hand on Haru’s shoulder. "The whole truth does not have to be the cruelest thing you can say," she said softly. "You can choose what stands out in the light."

Father Sota said nothing. He reached across the table and picked up the smallest carving knife. He held it out to Haru. The metal was cold and smooth.

"Cut away what does not belong," Father said. "Leave what is true standing."

Haru took the knife. It felt heavy in her palm, like a stone from the canal bed. She looked at the blank block of cherry wood beside it. She could carve the crack. She could carve the wind. She could carve the sparks. But she could leave out the boy. The truth could stand tall without a name.
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad man in a dark brown work coat, holds out a small carving knife to Haru, who stands in her rust-orange kimono with her hands outstretched, while Grandfather Tobei, in a blue-grey kimono, watches from the side, a blank wooden block resting on the table between them.

pages.text:
But leaving a name out was not enough. Haru knew that. She thought of Hachi, the bathhouse owner. She could hear his voice in her head, loud and rough. If he saw the word "furnace" on the sheet, he would be ashamed. And shame, Haru knew, was a thing that looked for a place to hide. He might blame Shin. He might send the boy away. Or worse, he might say nothing, and let the whole street believe the boy had been reckless.

Haru set the knife down. She picked up her little booklet. The paper was soft from her hands.

"I have to tell him first," she said.

"Tell him what?" Kichi asked.

"Tell him the truth," Haru said. "Before the ink touches the paper. Before the sellers go out. I have to stand in front of him and say it with my own mouth."

She tucked the booklet into her apron. Her heart was beating again, but this time it was not from fear. It was from purpose. She knew what she had to do. She had to be the first to speak the hard part.
pages.image: Haru, in her rust-orange kimono, holds a small folded booklet close to her chest with both hands, looking determined, while Kichi, in his moss-green coat, leans forward asking a question, the dim workshop around them with shelves of wooden blocks in the background.

pages.text:
The bathhouse looked like a dark, heavy shape in the grey morning light. Thin smoke still curled from the chimney. Haru pushed the door open, and it creaked loudly in the silence. The air inside smelled of wet stone and old water.

Hachi sat on a low beam near the changing area, his head buried in his hands. He wore his dark navy coat, and his thick eyebrows were furrowed tight. He did not look up when the door slid.

Haru took a step forward. Her voice came out small at first, barely louder than a mouse squeak.

"Master Hachi," she said.

He did not move. Haru took a deep breath, stood up straighter, and looked at the floor.

"I saw the crack in the chimney," she said, her voice steadier now. "I saw the wind push the sparks. I saw the ash door that would not close. And I saw Shin." She paused for a moment. "They were small things that happened together. It was not one person's fault."

Hachi lowered his head further into his palms, and his shoulders shook, just once, like a leaf in a sudden gust.

"It does not have to be one person's fault at all," Haru added.
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron, stands in the doorway of a dark, soot-stained bathhouse, speaking to Hachi, a gruff man with thick eyebrows in a dark navy coat, who sits with his head in his hands on a wooden beam, smoke curling from a chimney outside.

pages.text:
Hachi lifted his head. His eyes were red and swollen, the skin under them puffy and white. For a moment, he did not look like the big, loud man who ran the bathhouse. He looked like someone who had not slept in weeks.

"I have known about the crack since autumn," he said. His voice was rough, scraped raw by silence. "I was waiting for the wind to die. I was wrong."

He moved to stand, and then stopped. He looked past Haru, toward the shadowed corner by the wall where the light did not reach.

Shin was there.

The boy had been hiding in the dark. He stood up slowly. His soot-grey jacket was dusty, while his bare arms remained black with soot. He was trembling, his knees knocking together with a soft, wooden sound, but he stood very straight.

"It was me," Shin said. His voice was quiet but clear. "I left the door open. I was so tired."

He did not look at Haru. He looked at Hachi, and the old man looked back at him. The heavy silence in the room suddenly felt different. The weight lifted from Haru’s shoulders, leaving the air feeling thin and sharp.
pages.image: Two people and one child in a dim bathhouse doorway: Shin, a skinny nine-year-old boy in a soot-grey short jacket with arms black with soot, stands trembling but straight, Hachi, a man in a dark navy short coat with a towel over his shoulder, looks down at him with red wet eyes, and small Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron, stands in front of them looking up.
